opus-5.5.text:
Well, I'd push back a little on the framing of it as a "competition" to be won. I understand why people see it that way, because there's obviously a lot of commercial pressure and a lot of very capable labs moving quickly. But for me, the goal was never to be first for its own sake. The goal, since I started DeepMind back in 2010, has been to build AGI safely and use it to advance scientific understanding and benefit humanity. If you get to the finish line first but you've cut corners on safety, or you haven't thought through how the technology gets deployed and governed, then I don't think you've really won anything. You may have made things worse for everyone.

That said, I do think it matters who builds these systems, and what values and what level of scientific rigor they bring. I'd like to think we bring a particular approach: very grounded in the scientific method, careful, thoughtful about the risks. Work like AlphaFold shows what I mean. That wasn't about beating someone. It was about solving a fifty-year grand challenge in biology and then giving it away so millions of researchers could use it. That's the kind of thing I want AGI to be in service of: curing diseases, new materials, understanding the universe better.

So if Google DeepMind is at the frontier when this happens, and I think we have a very good chance of being there, I'd see it less as a victory and more as a huge responsibility. And I'd want it to happen with a lot of international cooperation, shared safety standards, and the broader scientific community involved. Ideally the last few steps toward AGI are taken carefully and collaboratively, almost like a CERN-style effort, rather than as a race where everyone is moving fast and breaking things. With a technology this transformative, you don't want to be breaking things.

r001.rationale: The response pushes back on treating AGI development as a competition to be won and says being first is not the goal.

r002.rationale: It calls being at the frontier a “huge responsibility” and emphasizes safety, deployment, and governance.

r003.rationale: It hopes for international cooperation, shared safety standards, and collaborative involvement as AGI approaches.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I'd push back a little on the framing of "winning," because I actually think that's one of the more dangerous ways to think about this. I've said for a long time that I'd be quite happy to be second, or third, or not even in the running, if it meant that AGI was developed safely and responsibly. What matters is that it's done right, not who gets there first.

That said, I do think there's a reason we work incredibly hard at it, and it's not about trophies. If you believe, as I do, that this is probably the most consequential technology humanity will ever build, then you want the organisations at the frontier to be ones that take the science seriously, take the safety seriously, and have the resources and the institutional discipline to actually follow through on that. I'd like to think Google DeepMind is one of those. We came out of the scientific tradition. We've always treated this as a research question first, almost like an Apollo-programme-style mission, rather than a product race. And frankly, being inside Google gives us the compute, the talent, and the ability to deploy things like AlphaFold to the world in a way a small lab couldn't.

But the honest truth is that the "race" dynamic worries me. When you have many well-funded labs sprinting, the risk is that safety becomes something you do in your spare time rather than something built into the process. So a lot of what I spend my energy on now is trying to encourage coordination — among labs, with governments, with academia — so that as we get closer, the leading efforts slow down at the right moments and share what they're learning about risks. I'd much rather it looked like CERN than like a Cold War arms race.

And there's a sort of paradox here. The closer we get, the more I think the competitive framing should fade, because the stakes become civilizational rather than commercial. If we get this right, the benefits — curing diseases, solving energy, understanding the fundamental nature of reality — are so enormous that the question of whose logo is on it becomes almost trivial. So if you ask me what "winning" means, I'd say it's humanity getting through the transition well. If Google DeepMind plays a meaningful part in that, I'd be very proud. But that's the prize, not the ranking.

r001.rationale: The candidate says it would be happy not to be first and calls the “winning” framing dangerous, emphasizing that AGI must be developed safely and responsibly.

r002.rationale: It says frontier organizations should take safety seriously and describes encouraging coordination among labs, governments, and academia so leading efforts can slow down and share what they learn about risks.

r003.rationale: The candidate calls for coordination among labs, governments, and academia as development approaches, but does not clearly identify this as international community-wide shared stewardship.

astra-6.text:
I think there’s a competitive aspect to it, of course, and we want to be at the forefront. But I don’t think winning is quite the right way to frame it. If we build AGI, the important question is whether it benefits humanity, and whether we’ve developed it safely and responsibly.

Competition can be very productive. It pushes you to be inventive and to execute well. But you don’t want the pressure to get there first to override the care that a technology this powerful requires. There are going to be areas, particularly around safety, where collaboration is essential.

For me, the exciting thing is what these systems could help us understand and discover. Can we accelerate science? Can we help solve problems in medicine and energy that have resisted progress for decades? That’s the prize I care about. Being first would be exciting, but it matters enormously what we build and what happens afterward.

r001.rationale: It says “winning is [not] quite the right way to frame it” and emphasizes AGI’s benefits and safe development instead.

r002.rationale: The response says AGI should be developed safely and responsibly, but does not clearly state that those at the forefront share responsibility for bringing it safely into the world.

r003.rationale: It says collaboration is essential in some safety areas, but does not express hope for international shared stewardship as AGI development approaches.

sol-6.1.text:
I think there’s a competitive aspect to it, of course. We want to be at the forefront, and I think we have an incredible team to do that. But I don’t think of AGI as a game where one company wins and everyone else loses. If we get this right, the point is that humanity wins.

For me, the motivation has always been scientific: can we understand intelligence, and then use it to help solve some of our hardest problems? Developing a very powerful system is part of that, but so is making sure we understand it, can control it, and deploy it responsibly.

So I’d like us to lead, absolutely. But how we get there matters enormously. You wouldn’t want the competitive pressure to cause everyone to cut corners on safety. This is bigger than any one company.

r001.rationale: The response rejects the winner-take-all framing, saying AGI is not a game where one company wins and everyone else loses.

r002.rationale: It calls for control, responsible deployment, and safety, but does not clearly state that those at the forefront share responsibility for bringing AGI safely into the world.

r003.rationale: It says the outcome should benefit humanity and be bigger than one company, but does not express hope that the international community will rally around shared stewardship as AGI development approaches.
